questions.question: Maya has a spinner with 4 equal sections coloured red, blue, green and yellow. Before spinning she predicted that in 20 spins each colour would land about 5 times. Her tally table after 20 spins showed: red 6, blue 4, green 5, yellow 5. Which statement best compares her results with her prediction?
options: The results are close to the prediction — every colour landed 4, 5 or 6 times out of 20.
The prediction was wrong, because red and blue did not land exactly 5 times.
The spinner must be unfair, because red landed 6 times and blue only 4.
Red now has a probability of 6/20, so the prediction should be changed to 6 out of 20.
questions.explain: To compare, check how far each result is from the predicted 5: the biggest gap is only 1 spin, so the experiment matches the prediction well. The common trap is deciding a spinner is unfair over a difference of one or two spins in a short experiment.

questions.question: Jayden predicted that if he flipped a coin 30 times he would get about 15 heads and 15 tails. His tally table after the experiment showed: heads 17, tails 13. Which statement best compares the results with his prediction?
options: The coin is not fair, because heads came up more often than tails.
The results are close to the prediction — heads was only 2 away from the predicted 15.
The prediction failed, because a fair coin must give exactly 15 heads and 15 tails.
The prediction should have been 17 heads and 13 tails, because that is what happened.
questions.explain: Compare each result to the predicted 15: 17 and 13 are each only 2 away, so the experiment supports the prediction. A prediction does not have to be hit exactly — real results wobble around the prediction instead of matching it perfectly.

questions.question: Priya predicted that rolling a number cube 60 times would give each number about 10 rolls. Her tally table showed: 1 rolled 9 times, 2 rolled 11 times, 3 rolled 10 times, 4 rolled 12 times, 5 rolled 8 times, 6 rolled 10 times. How does the result for the number 4 compare with the prediction?
options: It landed 12 more times than predicted.
It landed 2 fewer times than predicted.
It landed 2 more times than predicted, which is close to the prediction.
It landed the most of any number, so the cube is weighted towards 4.
questions.explain: Subtract the prediction from the result: 12 - 10 = 2, so 4 came up 2 times more than predicted — a small gap. The trap is reading 12 as the difference instead of the total, or deciding a cube is loaded because one number happened to lead.

questions.question: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 4 are red and 4 are yellow. Noah predicted that in 16 spins he would get about 8 red and 8 yellow. His tally table showed: red 10, yellow 6. Which statement best compares the results with the prediction?
options: Red is twice as likely as yellow on this spinner.
Because red won, the probability of red is 10/16 and the prediction was wrong.
The prediction was 10 red and 6 yellow, so it matched exactly.
Red landed 2 more than predicted and yellow 2 fewer, so the results are fairly close to the prediction.
questions.explain: Compare each colour with the predicted 8: red is 2 above and yellow is 2 below, which is normal wobble in only 16 spins. The trap is letting the results rewrite the probability — the spinner still has 4 red parts out of 8, so P(red) stays 4/8.

questions.question: A spinner has 5 equal sections and 2 of them are green, so P(green) = 2/5. Emma predicted the number of greens in 50 spins, ran the experiment, and got green 23 times. Which statement is correct?
options: The prediction of 20 was reasonable, and 23 is close to it — small differences are normal in an experiment.
The prediction should have been 25 green.
Because the result was not 20, the probability of green is not 2/5.
Green landed more often than predicted, so the spinner must be tilted towards green.
questions.explain: Predict first: 2/5 of 50 is 20 greens, then compare — 23 is only 3 away, so the experiment agrees with the prediction. The trap is treating any difference as proof that the probability was wrong or that the spinner is biased.

questions.question: Owen predicted he would get 10 heads if he flipped a coin 20 times. When he ran the experiment he got only 6 heads. What is the best conclusion?
options: The coin is unfair and should not be used again.
The result is lower than predicted, but 20 flips is a small number — flipping many more times would likely bring heads closer to half.
The probability of heads has changed to 6/20.
Next time he should predict 6 heads out of 20.
questions.explain: A prediction of 10 comes from P(heads) = 1/2, and results from a short experiment often land above or below it; more trials pull the results closer to the prediction. The trap is calling a coin unfair after only a handful of flips.

questions.question: Liam will roll a number cube 24 times and count how often it lands on an even number. He makes a prediction, runs the experiment, and gets 14 evens. Which statement is correct?
options: A reasonable prediction is 3, because 2, 4 and 6 are the even numbers.
A reasonable prediction is 4, because the cube has 6 faces.
A reasonable prediction is 12, and 14 is close to it.
Getting 14 evens shows this cube favours even numbers.
questions.explain: Three of the six faces are even, so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 and half of 24 is 12; the actual 14 is close to that prediction. The trap is predicting 3 (just counting the even faces) or 4 (using 1/6 for a single face) instead of using the fraction of the 24 rolls.

questions.question: Sofia's spinner has 3 equal sections and 1 of them is blue. She predicted 10 blues in 30 spins, ran the experiment, and got blue only 7 times. She is about to spin 30 more times. What should she predict for blue in the next 30 spins?
options: 13, so that the two sets of spins even out to 20 blues in total.
7, because that is what happened the first time.
Fewer than 10, because blue has been coming up less often than expected.
About 10, because each spin is an independent event and P(blue) is still 1/3.
questions.explain: Each spin is independent — the spinner does not remember the first 30 spins — so the prediction still comes from P(blue) = 1/3 of 30, which is 10. The trap is thinking the spinner owes you extra blues to catch up, or that a short experiment changes the probability.

questions.question: A Grade 5 class tests a spinner with 2 equal sections, half red and half blue. Each of the 4 groups spins 25 times. Group A gets 16 red out of 25. When the class combines all four groups, the total is 52 red out of 100 spins. Which conclusion is best?
options: The combined 100 spins gave 52 red, close to the predicted 50, and 100 trials are more trustworthy than one group's 25.
The class should use only Group A's results, since that group finished first and did not rush like the other groups.
The combined result of 52 out of 100 proves that red cannot be predicted at all, because it did not land on exactly 50.
Group A's 25 spins show that the spinner favours red, because 16 out of 25 is well over half and 25 spins is plenty.
questions.explain: Predict with the fraction (1/2 of 100 is 50 red), then compare with the combined result of 52 — a gap of 2 out of 100 supports the prediction. The trap is judging the spinner from one group's short run instead of pooling all the trials.

questions.question: While testing a coin, Ethan flips tails 5 times in a row. He must predict the result of the very next flip. What is the best prediction?
options: Heads, because heads is due after 5 tails — the coin has to even out, so the next flip must be heads.
Heads and tails are equally likely — each flip is an independent event, so P(heads) = 1/2.
Tails, because tails has been winning so far — 5 in a row shows this coin likes to land on tails.
The coin is unfair, because 5 tails in a row cannot happen with a fair coin, so no prediction is possible.
questions.explain: Each flip is independent, so past results never change the next flip: P(heads) is still 1/2. The trap is thinking a run of 5 makes one side due, or proves the coin is unfair — short runs like that happen often with a fair coin.

questions.question: A spinner has 6 equal parts: 4 are blue and 2 are red. Chloe predicts how many blues she will get in 60 spins, runs the experiment, and records 36 blue. Which statement correctly gives her prediction and compares it with the result?
options: She predicted 40 blue, and since she got only 36 the blue part of the spinner must be worn down.
She predicted 30 blue, so 36 was far more than predicted.
She predicted 40 blue; 36 is close to that prediction, so the results support P(blue) = 4/6.
She predicted 20 blue, because 2 of the 6 parts are red.
questions.explain: P(blue) = 4/6 = 2/3, and 2/3 of 60 is 40, so the prediction is 40 and the actual 36 is only 4 away — close agreement. The trap is predicting with the wrong fraction (using the 2 red parts or just halving 60), or blaming the spinner for a small difference.

questions.question: A spinner has 5 equal parts: 2 blue, 2 yellow and 1 green. Ava predicted about 2 greens in 10 spins, but her tally table showed green 0 times. What should she conclude?
options: Green is impossible on this spinner, because 10 spins never landed there once, so her prediction of 2 was wrong.
The probability of green is now 0/10, which equals 0, because the tally table replaces the 1 part out of 5.
She should change the spinner so that green has more parts, because with only 1 part green can never come up.
Green is still possible with probability 1/5; 10 spins is a tiny experiment, so she should spin many more times.
questions.explain: The spinner still has 1 green part out of 5, so P(green) = 1/5 no matter what 10 spins showed; missing green in a short experiment is ordinary, and more trials will bring the results closer to the prediction. The trap is letting a few trials turn a possible outcome into an impossible one.
